video_title: Richard Hanania on Conrad’s Nostromo, Latin American Crime, and Populism
transcript: TYLER COWEN: Hello, everyone, and welcome back  to Conversations with Tyler. Today, I am sitting   here live in Arlington with Richard Hanania, whose  name I often cannot pronounce entirely correctly.   Richard has a new book out called Kakistocracy:  Why Populism Ends in Disaster. I’m happy to   have blurbed that book. A lot of the book is  about the stupidity of our current politics. I decided I was rather sick of the stupidity  of our current politics, so I said to Richard,   “Why don’t we talk about some other stupidities  instead?” We decided jointly we would start   off the conversation by discussing Joseph  Conrad’s Nostromo, a book which I reread,   and he was reading, I think, for the  first time. Here we are. Richard, welcome. RICHARD HANANIA: It’s a pleasure, Tyler, and I  think that was an excellent selection. I think   you showed your genius by picking it because it’s  perfect for what we’re going to talk about today. COWEN: Do you want to start by  just giving a very brief sense of   where Nostromo starts? What is it  about? Where does the novel open? HANANIA: Yes. It’s in a fictional Latin American  country called Costaguana. I think of it as a   combination of Colombia, and maybe Argentina,  Mexico, and maybe Venezuela. You’re focusing on   something called the Occidental Province, which is  the West coast of the country, so it’s facing the   Pacific Ocean. You basically have this mine that  is central to that region. It revolves around a   man named Charles Gould, who’s an Englishman, but  who has roots in Costaguana, who runs the mine. He and other, what Conrad calls, material  interests, so basically Western money men,   are invested in the country. They’re supporting  some conservative moderate regime that is letting   them develop the country. There’s an uprising  basically led by the minister of defense named   Montero. That’s the basic conflict of the  book. The title [character], Nostromo, is   a seaman. He works for the ONS shipping  company, which is one of the Western   interests. A lot of the story revolves around  him and his relationship with Giorgio Viola,   who’s a hotel proprietor in the city,  and then also his wife and two daughters. COWEN: I’ll add just a bit to that. This  novel comes out in 1904. It’s published   in serialized form. Today, it’s typically  considered to be Conrad’s greatest novel.   I think I agree with that assessment. It was  the British literary critic F. R. Leavis who   really resurrected the reputation of  this book, which for a long time was   ignored. It’s not short. In my edition, it’s  about 560 pages. I find it difficult to read,   but it’s one of my favorite novels. It would be  in, say, my favorite 50, maybe even my favorite   30. There’s a lot of different moving pieces. The  story does not always come in synchronous form.   It’s just, on purpose, a complicated story  because the world is a complicated world. HANANIA: Yes. This is where you’re happy to have  AI because you could put things in there, and you   could say, “What does this mean? What is it about  this? What is this again?” Even the geography,   I thought, the first 30 pages or so, where it’s  telling you what Costaguana is, because all this   stuff is going to be very relevant for the plot.  I Googled Costaguana. What is a map? You got a   nice map online. Yes, you read it with some  aids to actually understand what’s going on. COWEN: I’ll give you my answer afterward, but  tell me, you reading this for the first time   and then hearing it again on audiobook,  what most struck you about it? Maybe the   word surprise is a little too strong, but what  peaks your attention so much about Nostromo? HANANIA: The political angle, I thought, was very  interesting in that I think of Latin American   dysfunction to be caused by socialism ideas  that started to take off in the 20th century,   in the second half of the 20th century. It is so  modern, even though the word socialism doesn’t   appear in the book until near the very end, or not  even the concept of socialism in any real sense. Basically, you have these Western interests.  They’re doing things in the country. We’ll get   to this. I think it’s a very pro-business  book. Maybe I think a little bit of an   Ayn Rand with less caffeine or something like  that. It’s more realistic, more of a realist   novel. Yes, just how recognizable it is for anyone  who knows anything about Latin American history. COWEN: The way I read Conrad, he’s clearly not  a socialist, but he views socialism as more of   a symptom than a cause. There’s this dead hand  of history and rent seeking and plutocracy and   corruption. Socialism is a particular later  form of that. Basically, the place is trapped,   and how effectively he portrays a trapped  society in a world where a lot of countries do   not develop very effectively. Though published  in 1904, again, to me also seemed remarkably   topical. If you were doing development  economics and you were to send people,   say, to five novels, A House for Mr. Biswas,  a few others, this would be one of the five. HANANIA: Yes, I think that’s right. It’s  a timeless lesson in that these countries,   they need Western capital and Western  expertise in order to develop. The   problem is there’s nothing politically  less popular than just a bunch of rich   foreigners coming around and doing a bunch of  things. That’s easier to demagogue. That’s the   balance. It’s like the mind is bringing  development. It’s beloved in the region,   at least for the time. Whether that’s the case  in the long run, that’s one of the lessons of   the book. Then, at the same time, it’s just all  the discourse surrounding what’s going on there   is just hostile. They’re constantly fending off  threats to that ability to develop the country. COWEN: Here’s one thing that struck me, and I’m  not sure you’ll agree. Early in the novel, there’s   all this talk about the Italians and Garibaldi and  liberty, and the extent to which I think this book   is also a critique of classical liberalism is what  surprised me reading it for the second time. The   first time was probably, I guess, 30 years ago,  that Conrad is not against the classical liberal   prescription, really, but he views it as another  pathology inserted into a hopeless situation. It just morphs into some form of corruption and  interest groups. It’s replaced by the autocrats,   but it turns out to not really  matter more. There’s, again,   this dead hand of history. The indigenous  groups, their customs, their norms are   really what rule the area. The foreigners come  and go, and they may steal or extract wealth,   but at the end of the day, the talk of  liberty and democracy, for him, it’s a   kind of fraud. I think it’s also a recognition  that imperialism was not going to do the job. HANANIA: Don’t you think that the Occidental  Province had a higher GDP per capita than the   rest of the country? It wasn’t just they made  money. It seems like there was real wealth.   Getting to the end, to the spoilers,  the miners actually march on the city   because they’re so loyal to Gould. They  like what’s going on. There is actual   improvement in people’s lives.  It’s not that nihilistic, right? COWEN: It may be higher GDP, but keep  in mind GNP may be what counts. I don’t   think Conrad thought in those terms. I  don’t read him as a consequentialist,   though I’m mostly one myself. For  him, progress is about moral progress.   He doesn’t see a lot of moral progress in this  setting. The point that that’s not happening is,   for him, at least more important than,  oh, living standards went up a bit or,   well, isn’t this better than the even poorer  societies they had earlier on? I think he grew   up in what we now call Poland, but then was ruled  by Russia. The idea of foreign rule is something   he had such a strong instinctive dislike of. And  you see it in his other books as well that he’s   a cynic about foreign presence, though I don’t  think he’s saying things were better before. HANANIA: No, I don’t think I agree. COWEN: I didn’t think you would  agree. That’s why I said that. HANANIA: There is a noble savage idea. There’s  one part where he goes into the rant when Sotillo,   the general, is torturing Hirsch. I  think he goes into a rant about how   primitive man did not devise as much sadistic  torture, which I don’t think is probably true,   but that’s Conrad’s idea. Basically,  there’s a kind of innocence there. I look at the Hernandez and the robbers and the  people who are living in the countryside. Those   people are purest case of noble savage. There is  part of that. You’re right. Conrad is into honor.   This is a book about love and men caring about  women. There’s Monygham, the doctor’s loyalty   to Mrs. Gould, and then Decoud’s loyalty to  Antonia. His other books are about this. Yes,   he’s a romantic. He’s not a romantic in  politics. He thinks politics is a dirty— COWEN: Agreed. HANANIA: —unromantic world. If he thinks  socialism and populism on a scale of one   to 10 are like a one and classical liberalism  is a four, to me, he’s a classical liberal,   even though he’s not an eight or  a nine on classical liberalism. COWEN: I think I read him as believing in  contingency as the most important truth   of politics and a geographic relativism. I  don’t think he has much Rousseau in him of   idealizing the noble savages, but he sees the  noble savages are not noble. They’re terrible,   but what’s terrible in them gets  recreated in us at higher levels   of wealth and power. That, for him, is  the most fundamental truth of politics. HANANIA: There’s more of that  in the Heart of Darkness,   which is about a guy who just goes crazy  and becomes worse than the worst savage. COWEN: It’s more explicit, I think. HANANIA: Yes. Is it here, though? Is Gould a  savage? I think they come across well. I think   compared to the demagogues, compared  to the Montero, these half-literate,   various kind of guys who go around torturing  people and just trying to grab as much wealth   as possible—like Gould, what’s his biggest flaw?  He’s not emotionally expressive. There’s the sins   of the Western material interests just pale  in comparison to what the alternative is. COWEN: I think Mrs. Gould comes across as fine.  Mr. Gould just seems captured by where he’s   lived for, what, now three generations. He’s a  pretend Englishman. I think it’s Conrad poking   fun at people who are actually Englishmen and  have not lived abroad for three generations,   but pointing out how quickly they  become corrupted by the places they go,   which for him would include Malaya,  India, many other locations. HANANIA: What would a noncorrupt Gould  look like? What would he have done? COWEN: Mrs. Gould is the noncorrupt Gould.  Again, I think she’s fine and nice enough— HANANIA: Could she run the mine? COWEN: —but has no power. No. HANANIA: She couldn’t run the mine,   though. You won’t get a mine if  you won’t have someone like Gould. COWEN: That’s right. That’s the contrast. HANANIA: Can you run the mine and be better  than Gould in the way his wife is? No. It’s   a tragic situation, unquestionably. This  isn’t Ayn Rand. There’s so many hints of   it. I don’t know what Conrad’s influence  on Rand was, but this idea that we’re going   to destroy the world and break it down with  it, she must have gotten it from him, right? I don’t know if it’s convergent evolution,  but it’s not as cartoonish. It is still   this man who can accomplish great things and  wants to be left alone. He doesn’t cheat his   workers. He doesn’t steal their money. He  doesn’t whip them. There’s none of this   other stuff that you find in people who  are more skeptical of Western interests. COWEN: Keep in mind, the novel is named  Nostromo, not Gould. He’s the central   character. One thing that struck me is how  he has four different names. The first one,   Nostromo, it’s like nos, our man, you could  say, out of Italian and Latin. He’s presented   as our man. He turns out to be a fraud. He  doesn’t mind the notion of killing Hirsch or,   oh, if he’s tortured, maybe we don’t  really need to do that. He won’t bless   Mrs. Viola. He’s a bastard. He cares about  his own reputation. He becomes a thief. His real name, Gianni Battista, gets  forgotten that he’s, in fact, from Italy,   is part of what’s forgotten in the novel,  just like Gould being originally English is   forgotten. For a while, he’s called Capataz  de Cargadores. He’s the man of capacity. He   gets things done. The novel’s always poking  fun at that version of Nostromo. Finally,   he’s called Captain Fidanza, captain of  faith. All the belief in him, all along,   was just that of faith. He’s a rotten guy  who’s a thief and doesn’t mind killing people. HANANIA: Is he a rotten guy? COWEN: He’s a rotten guy. HANANIA: I don’t know. Is he a rotten guy? I  think Conrad admires him. He’s an antihero, right? COWEN: Conrad always has a bit  of sympathy for the antihero. HANANIA: You’re right. He’s a thief, but it’s the  most understandable, sympathetic kind of thievery   you can imagine. Everyone thinks this thing is  sunk. He’s basically sacrificed himself. He’s   vain. I think that’s his problem. He’s vain.  This is not seen, I think, as much of a sin in   Conrad’s time as it would be today. There’s  this idea that people basically care about   the reputation of others. It’s not like Battista  or Nostromo runs away from that. He admits that. Then Viola, the wife, Teresa, thinks  he’s just a fool for this. Still,   it’s presented as an acceptable kind of  morality. There’s not a sadistic streak.   He’s poor. He’s poor up until the point  he gets tempted by the silver. He’s not   motivated by these venial concerns like these  generals are. He’s not self-sacrificial. He’s   not a saint or anything. I thought he was  a good guy. I don’t think he was a bad guy. COWEN: No, I think he’s a bad guy.  Teresa has the best critique of him. Oh,   you just care what people think of you. People  are paid to praise you. You’re really a fraud,   she basically says. I think Conrad is showing  us he’s a victim of the place he moves to,   and he’s not any worse than what surrounds him.  He is, in essence, swallowed up by that world,   by the silver mine, by the culture surrounding  him. Just as Kurtz goes evil in Heart of Darkness,   Nostromo is in a less evil place, but he  goes corrupt. I think this is something,   maybe in a way, we’re supposed  to accept but not approve of. HANANIA: I don’t know. What would virtue look like  to Conrad in someone in Nostromo’s situation? I   think that actually being brave, being the kind  of person that people look up to for a reason,   his reputation is an earned kind of reputation.  He’s known for being this guy who seduces women   and is brave and is taking care of  people. It’s the opposite of a toxic   masculinity. It’s a healthier masculinity  when you compare it to the other people   in the region. I think Nostromo is not an  intellectual, he’s not somebody like that, but   someone whose instincts and heart are basically  in the right place. I disagree strongly on this. COWEN: His involvement with women, to me,   is a negative. He’s considering the two  Viola daughters. They’re called girls, right? HANANIA: Yes. COWEN: Now, your views on this may  not be the normal current views. HANANIA: How old are they at the end,  by the way, when he’s about to marry? COWEN: We don’t know. They’re called  girls and there is some passage of time,   but they’re not that old. I read Nostromo  again, this is guessing, as being in his   30s. He’s maybe a 37-year-old. He doesn’t  really relate to either girl as a human being. HANANIA: This is the turn of the century. COWEN: That Conrad is disapproving, and  it’s superficial, I think. There were   real love relationships in the story  elsewhere, even the Goulds, right? HANANIA: Oh, yes. COWEN: Or Decoud and the woman he’s in love  with. Nostromo has the worst relationship to   women. It’s all mediated through the father.  He treats the two as interchangeable. He’ll   pick at some point. He doesn’t love them. He  doesn’t care that they don’t love him. It’s at   best transactional or rooted in some desire for  sex or domination. Again, I think Conrad is not   simply a moralizing author, but he’s observing and  showing, and he’s not asking us to admire this. HANANIA: No, I don’t think he’s asking us to  admire what’s going on with the girls. Yes,   you’re right. That’s a good point about  contrasting the relationships. I still   look at this as basically Nostromo’s  vain, stop the presses. We know that,   right? He’s not out there. There are worse  things you can be, right? You can imagine   someone being even worse with women. He  seems to want to leave them better off. That one scene that there’s a striking  scene in the beginning where she’s like,   “Aren’t you my love, Nostromo, iron-red girl?”  My reading of that scene is that basically,   he wants to elevate her status. It’s a girl, maybe  he’s not in love with [her]. It’s not a big deal,   but he wants to make her feel good, and  he wants to give her the privilege of   having known Nostromo. He’s not sacrificing  his life to her and making her a wife and   having a traditional family and all that  stuff. Again, he’s vain. He’s a Playboy.   His heart is in the right place. I don’t  think there’s some terrible sin in that. I think the Linda thing, where  he chooses the younger daughter,   I think it’s him being vain and wanting to  be unfettered. I feel like he was thinking   she was going to nag him for the rest  of his life. She loved him too much,   right? He wasn’t trying to hurt anyone, though.  He’s a limited character, but not a bad guy. COWEN: Let me read you a quotation from  Charles Gould, which I think is important,   and you tell me what you think of it.  I quote, “He would blow everything up   from loyalty and from hate, from hate of  those liberals, as they call themselves,   liberals. The words one knows so well have a  nightmarish meaning in this country. Liberty,   democracy, patriotism, government, all of  them have a flavor of folly and murder.” I think that’s Conrad telling us what  he thinks. Conrad wants to be a liberal,   broadly is a liberal, left Russian tyranny for  England, preferred England, but he goes around   the world, and he sees what those principles  are translating into, and he thinks that it   all does have the flavor of folly and murder.  What’s your take on that passage and my view? HANANIA: I think you’re right. That is Conrad’s  view. Does that mean he thinks classical   liberalism is something that you shouldn’t  even bother trying to bring to the Third World,   or that’s something that is destined to end  terribly? I don’t know if it’s that cynical.   He has this phrase called Negro liberalism,  which I’d never heard before, which I’m not   sure exactly what it’s supposed to mean, but  to me that strikes me as it’s a bastardization. If you want to put it in modern terms, it’s  like classical liberals not liking leftists   calling something liberal. I think probably,  maybe the best case against what you’re saying   is José Avellanos. That, I think, is the most  uncomplicated, probably the best character   in the story. Conrad, in this very  strange forward, which sounds real,   but is obviously made up, where he says  the author read the history of Avellanos,   and that’s the basis. This guy is just a good  guy, and he likes Gould, he likes the mine,   he likes classical liberalism. I see  him as the conscience of the novel. COWEN: Here’s, I think, a point where we  disagree. First, a side remark. Supposedly,   there’s a Venezuelan author called Ramón Pérez  where the concept of Negro liberalism came   from him and he was presenting it in a way  similar to what you describe. I think Conrad   has a quite ironic twist on this. Here’s the  passage concerning Avellanos and I’m quoting,   “The clamor of this Negro Liberalism”—capital  letters Negro Liberalism—“frightened Señor   Avellanos. A newspaper was the  only remedy.” Conrad is mocking. It’s like, oh, we have a newspaper in  response, but the classical liberals are   just as absurd. The newspaper, as you know,  is called Porvenir, Spanish word for future,   which is again just mocking. I think he’s  taking the people who are worried about   what they were calling Negro liberalism,  and just saying the classical liberals,   they’re in their own dream world, like,  “I’m sort of on their side, but come on,   get real. Look at what’s actually happening here.  They’re running around like a bunch of fools.” HANANIA: I think maybe we’re not  that far in disagreement. I think   we’re just emphasizing different  things. To me, it’s comparative,   right? They’re fools. They have  too much faith in newspapers. COWEN: Decoud kills himself, right? HANANIA: Yes. COWEN: He’s also broadly liberal,  most of all, a rationalist. HANANIA: That’s an interesting one because  that’s another issue. What I was going to say   is you compare them to the alternative. At one  point General Montero says he learned to read   just enough to read the newspapers and know  he was a great general who did great things,   and he wasn’t getting his respect, right?  They’re nasty. They have no ideas. They just   want to grab. They’re vain. They’re cowardly  too. Sotillo, the way he kills Hirsch,   the way he thinks about hiding under his desk at  one point. They don’t have any virtues at all. These are the political leadership. These are  the people who get to the top of the army. These   are the ones who demagogue. These are the ones  who draw the crowds. He has them behaving like   buffoons. I like that scene where they’re talking  about the men with many teeth, and then the other   one goes, “Oh, and he’s also a dentist.” I’m  not sure what that means, but it’s just funny. Yes, these are people with  flaws, all of them, but just,   my God, the domestic, organic political  leadership that emerges in Costaguana,   it’s just a horror show. That’s what strikes  me. All the other stuff that he says about   the material interests and the Westerners  and how silly they are, I take it all in,   but just from a comparative perspective, yes,  it’s obvious that the other side is much worse. COWEN: You’re such a comparativist. This  may come from your background in political   science. But also being a modern, facing political  choices, I don’t think Conrad is. I think he’s   more interested in showing us a fundamentally  tragic nature of reality and comparativism,   correctly or not, it’s the last thing  he wants to bring into the question. He is like Shakespeare, in fact. Shakespeare  is rarely debating the different kings he   writes about, were they better or worse than  some other king would have been? He’s trying   to teach us something about the situations  people are in. That’s also how I read Conrad,   is quite Shakespearean. You’re  a comparativist, which is fine,   but that’s maybe accounting for some of  the different ways we’re reading this book. HANANIA: Yes, possibly. It is his most political  novel, at least of the ones that I’ve read,   although The Secret Agent is political too. Yes,  Nostromo’s deepest interest isn’t politics. It   is humanity. It is honor. It is bonds that  bring people together across the world. There   is an implicit political vision in there.  All these books are about—and this follows   his life—people who go out there. Not all of his  books, but at least three of the big novels are   people who go out there. They have an adventure.  They’re meeting people from different races and   different backgrounds. They are experiencing  something. Everything is tragic. There is an   implicit politics behind that, but I agree with  you, the human factor is first and foremost. COWEN: I read Secret Agent, among other things,   but it’s being about how pathetic  and menial these terrorists are. Oh,   they’re assassins. You think it’s supposed to be  exciting, and it’s just a crummy story of idiots. HANANIA: Yes, I think that’s right. I’m  trying to get what the lesson is of The   Secret Agent. There was a news story at the  time that it was pretty much the same thing.   They were trying to blow up the exact  place that was getting blown up. Yes,   it’s just a tragedy. The story of the wife  in that story, the way—maybe we’re giving   away too many spoilers for this one, too—but  yes, I found the ending to that very tragic. COWEN: Yes. Now, why is Nostromo told in  such a manner where it does not have a   normal synchronization of the narrative?  Time shifts radically pretty frequently.   It’s one reason why it can be hard  to read. Why is it done that way? HANANIA: Yes, Conrad’s books are mostly  like this. There’s a few that are, I think,   chronological. Yes, I was thinking about  this, and it’s fun for me. I don’t know.   You said it was difficult. It was fun for  me to figure out, like, “Wait a minute,   where are we in the timeline here? Oh, wait, that  was last night,” but that was literally the first   page of the book, and now we’re near the end of  the book. It is, I think, a fun way to do it. Also, I think that there’s a meta story in  here about how Conrad thinks we look at events.   At the end, one of the most striking things when  he’s talking about Captain Mitchell at the end,   and Captain Mitchell, how he tells the  story of what happened to people in the   years after the revolution and the years after  the Occidental Province got its independence.   The way he tells the story is basically like  they can’t even keep up with what he’s saying.   They have no idea. He’s referencing things.  He’s like, “I’m going to get back to you on   this,” and they don’t even know what the  point is or who these characters are. I guess in retrospect, it just all looks  like a jumble, and it’s like that when   you’re reading it too. I guess the idea would  be for someone who’s unromantic about politics,   it seems like there’s a straight line, but  what’s the headline going to be in 10 years,   20 years, when someone looks back on this  story? It’s just going to be a jumble,   and they’re going to remember maybe  one or two things about what happened. COWEN: There’s no God, really, religion,   or priests in this story either. In  general, in Conrad, there’s not, right? HANANIA: Yes. COWEN: What do you make of that? For me, it’s  the point about tragedy again. That religion   really doesn’t matter, so why even put it  into the story? You would think, “Well,   this is a Spanish colony with a changing  political status. There’s an indigenous   religion. There’s a Catholic church.”  This is completely pushed offstage, right? HANANIA: It does appear in a very  strange place at the end when they   say Nostromo becomes religious,  and he’s attending mass. What do   you make of this? I was confused about  this. I didn’t know what to do with it. COWEN: Another source of being foolish? I don’t   know. We know Conrad himself was not a  believer and paid no heed to religion. HANANIA: It would have been unusual. Religion  was not a factor. We didn’t have the religious   right or something like that back then, right? The  major forces in politics were kings. There were   these anarchists and socialists. There were still  the classical liberals. There was nationalism. COWEN: I think it was state religion.  It was all pretty religious, at least   in superficial ways. How many people  believed exactly what, I’m not sure. HANANIA: There’s Avellano’s father, Corbelán.  Is that how you say his name? There is   this little side plot where, yes,  it’s not represented as anything   noble or anything interesting. It’s just  a way to be reactionary and to look for   opportunities to advance the interests of  the church at the expense of the people.   There is a little bit of religion. I  don’t think it’s portrayed very well. COWEN: In Heart of Darkness, Kurtz is setting  himself up as a god or godlike being. It’s   what happens when you have a religious vacuum,  and it’s maybe also Conrad telling us what he   thinks of religion, that it’s domination, and  he’s just not crazy about it. It’s striking,   the novel’s perspective on religion.  It also makes it quite modern, right? HANANIA: Yes. This is the thing about  Conrad. I really like a lot that’s in   there. I like the storytelling. I like the  extent that there’s politics in there. I   like the way it portrayed honor. Yes, it’s a  little bit too much for my taste. There’s no   redemption. I love Lord Jim. Again, I don’t want  to spoil people who are just getting into Conrad,   but I love the way that story unfolds.  The romance of the individual and his   principles and his passions is the  replacement for the politics, right? I do love that. Even though I’m a person who’s  into politics, I think that politics should   be a lot less romantic, and we should get  these sources of meaning from our day-to-day   lives. They have 10 different studies   that you’ve never read. They know more about a  topic than you have, so they’re actually very   difficult to argue with, but AI is just going  to sit there and take apart their points one by   one. It’s not going to condescend to them. It’s  not going to tell them that they’re idiots. Yes,   I think optimistic AI could actually help us here.  There might be the technology of the last 25,   probably 30, 40 years, probably going  back to cable news and talk radio,   and then social media took off. Maybe with  AI, it goes back in the other direction. COWEN: Who is the content creator on the  populist right who is most insightful,   most worth reading, most valuable? HANANIA: On the populist  right, who is most insightful? COWEN: Not classical liberal right. Not centrist. HANANIA: Are you including new  right people or just anyone? COWEN: I don’t even know what the  phrase new right means anymore,   but name some names, and  we’ll see if I think they fit. HANANIA: Steve Sailer. He’s playing the hits  in recent years, phoning it in, but I think   the basics of Sailerism, or I think he was ahead  of the trans issue. Helen Andrews, I like some of   her stuff. I think that some of the stuff has the  flaws of right-wing, starting with the conclusion   and then looking for the story. I wasn’t a big fan  of the feminization stuff, but some of the stuff   on inner city crime and stuff like that, I think,  is good. Let’s see. Who else? Dominic Cummings.   I think he’s more sympathetic to these people  than he is to a lot of other people in politics. COWEN: Those are three picks. What in your  model of the world is making them better,   them and the others, if you had a longer  list than the ones you think are worse? HANANIA: My least favorite thing in the  world—I’ve been thinking about this a lot. To me,   the lowest form of bias is partisan bias. Like  me and you are biased. Everyone has biases. Maybe   we’re biased in a classical liberal direction.  Maybe we read Conrad in a certain way. To me,   when you are biased in the direction of “my  side is right” on the political spectrum,   you’re abdicating being an intellectual.  You’re just giving your mind over to the mob. I think a lot of the right-wing stuff, it’s not  necessarily that it loves Trump. Sometimes it   is that. That’s the lower-grade version of it.  They hate liberals so much that there’s so much   motivated reasoning that the bias is always,  “Liberals are terrible people, and they’re   doing evil things.” I think that’s the problem. I  look for a little bit of independence, where you   don’t see that, where it’s just a one-sided  story about how terrible these people are. COWEN: This is June 2026. If the populist right  is so terrible, why is the stock market so high? HANANIA: Well, the question  is, could it be better? COWEN: Of course, it could be better, but  in absolute terms, aren’t things okay? HANANIA: Yes. We are the center of the AI  boom. Now, there was an Economist [article],   I think it might have been a cover story, where  we’re saying the Trump tax—they took the Trump   tax and they said, “AI is doing great. At the  same time, the Trump tax is basically tariffs   and immigration.” I’m like, “Wait a minute,  you’re going to detract immigration and tariffs,   but you’re not going to give him credit for the  AI boom?” He didn’t have to take this perspective   on AI. There were people who wanted to do a lot  more government control over what was going on. Yes, look, the right-wing populists we know are  better than left-wing populists just because   they have better economic ideas. Trumpism  is a combination of libertarianism and this   kind of retrograde nationalism and nativism,  but also just personal corruption. It might   work out economically. The benefits of just  letting AI go might overwhelm everything else.   There is a part of me that is like  Conrad. There’s an honor thing, right? When I watch these cabinet meetings—and there  was a New York Times analysis where like one in   five sentences or something are praising  Trump or attacking his enemies—there’s   something degrading about that. Maybe it  works out economically. I’m still open to   the idea that maybe Trump winning in 2024 was  better for the stock market in the long run,   but we can’t be that utilitarian. There’s  a point where we have to draw the line. COWEN: Why do conservative women hug  and liberal women shake your hand? HANANIA: I like that. That’s funny. The liberal  women, I think, there are norms. It’s not just   the liberal women. It’s the men. The men are  less flirtatious. They’re less aggressive. I   think the HR norms are more dominant among  liberals. I think as conservatives become   more self-consciously anti-liberal, they lean  into the other direction. You see women these   days in right-wing circles just being  open that they want to marry a rich guy. I think if you were a Republican  politico 30 years ago, 20 years ago,   it wasn’t that explicit. They were more  conforming to the norms of whatever person   who’s reading the Washington Post  and listening to NPR. There’s just   this divergence in values. The right is  leaning into human nature. The left is   leaning into this refined understanding of  sexuality and relations between the sexes. COWEN: Aren’t the right-wing men more bimodally  distributed that they’re either like Trump,   we know what that is, or they’re quite  honorable because they like Mitt Romney?   The men on the left, they’re much more likely  to be hypocritical. There’s more Bill Clintons   on the left. I’m not saying they all are by any  means. A lot are just loyally married. You look   at well-educated Democratic men, they have pretty  awesome demographic results in terms of marriages,   children, education, income. The right-wing  men just are weird all over the map? HANANIA: Yes. When you said bimodal,  you said some are like Trump,   and some are like Romney. I thought you were  going to say some were incels and shut-ins. I think that gets at something in  that the left-wing people just do   seem to be more conformist. It’s  like 1960s beatniks. You think,   “They’re the people challenging the system.”  No. At some point, liberalism became the   establishment. If you’re a person who is just  conforming to the dominant ideas of your society,   you’re going to be a liberal. Part of that is  probably monogamy and not being too much of a cad. I was surprised when I went to graduate school. I  thought wokeness was this surface thing that maybe   a few crazy people believed in. Little things like  ethics rules, like the IRB. I remember being in   grad school, and I remember not feeling any moral  obligation to do the ethics review before I did   a survey or something, but then people around me  would actually take it seriously. I’m like, “Wow,   these people are different than I am.” I’m sure  the Trump administration people are not like that. COWEN: I once wrote a post called “How Public  Intellectuals Can Extend Their Shelf Lives.”   You’ve written a book on populism. The future  of populism is uncertain. It could die out,   or it could just be everything becomes populist.  In a sense, in that scenario, maybe you can’t   just keep on writing books about populism.  Where do you see your own emphasis headed? HANANIA: I’ve reinvented myself on more than  one occasion. I’m always developing. I have   three books. The first one is on foreign policy.  The second one is civil rights law. The third   one is this one on populism. Yes, I don’t know  what I’m going to be at in two or three years. I do like fiction. To go back to the  Shakespeare thing, I do want to try   my hand at it. I’ve written two fictional  essays, and they were both big hits. Maybe   I want to take up fiction at some point. I  don’t know. I never know exactly. I read,   I think, I observe events, and  then I just go in a direction. COWEN: Does writing books still make sense? HANANIA: Makes sense from what? From a   knowledge-producing perspective or  from an individual’s perspective? COWEN: Either. HANANIA: From an individual’s perspective,  I think it does. If you want my thought on   different issues, it’s fragmented in  different places. There’s a tweet here   and there. There’s an essay here and there.  There’s an op-ed here and there. I see my   books as a consolidation of ideas that I’ve been  thinking about. Each one of my three books was   basically what I’ve been thinking about the  last two, three years, how I synthesize it,   and what I think are the nuggets there that are  really, really important that people should get. From my perspective, it makes sense. Also,  provides a reason for people to talk about you and   get you on podcasts and things like that. It makes  sense just from an intellectual level and from a   promotional level. Then, as a knowledge-producing  device, I’m not sure. I’m not sure if it ever did.   Maybe we should all just be reading bullet  points like Axios or something like that.   It still makes sense for an individual  who’s trying to get his ideas out there. COWEN: Final question. What in particular  do you wish to learn about next? HANANIA: This sounds completely random. I  do want to do a month on quantum physics. I   mentioned that in passing on the Substack. I had  two or three smart physicists reach out and say,   “If you need anything, reach out to us.”  I think there’s philosophical implications   there. I don’t know what they are. I don’t  know what direction I’ll go in. I feel like   this is something, at a deep level, I have  to have an opinion about. At some point,   I’m going to take two or three months, and  I’m going to really dig into it. Maybe I’ll   learn nothing. Maybe my brain cannot comprehend.  At least I need to try once in my life. COWEN: Richard, thank you very much. HANANIA: It’s a pleasure, Tyler.

transcript_segments.text: TYLER COWEN: Hello, everyone, and welcome back  to Conversations with Tyler. Today, I am sitting
here live in Arlington with Richard Hanania, whose  name I often cannot pronounce entirely correctly.
Richard has a new book out called Kakistocracy:  Why Populism Ends in Disaster. I’m happy to
have blurbed that book. A lot of the book is  about the stupidity of our current politics.
I decided I was rather sick of the stupidity  of our current politics, so I said to Richard,
“Why don’t we talk about some other stupidities  instead?” We decided jointly we would start
off the conversation by discussing Joseph  Conrad’s Nostromo, a book which I reread,
and he was reading, I think, for the  first time. Here we are. Richard, welcome.
RICHARD HANANIA: It’s a pleasure, Tyler, and I  think that was an excellent selection. I think
you showed your genius by picking it because it’s  perfect for what we’re going to talk about today.
COWEN: Do you want to start by  just giving a very brief sense of
where Nostromo starts? What is it  about? Where does the novel open?
HANANIA: Yes. It’s in a fictional Latin American  country called Costaguana. I think of it as a
combination of Colombia, and maybe Argentina,  Mexico, and maybe Venezuela. You’re focusing on
something called the Occidental Province, which is  the West coast of the country, so it’s facing the
Pacific Ocean. You basically have this mine that  is central to that region. It revolves around a
man named Charles Gould, who’s an Englishman, but  who has roots in Costaguana, who runs the mine.
He and other, what Conrad calls, material  interests, so basically Western money men,
are invested in the country. They’re supporting  some conservative moderate regime that is letting
them develop the country. There’s an uprising  basically led by the minister of defense named
Montero. That’s the basic conflict of the  book. The title [character], Nostromo, is
a seaman. He works for the ONS shipping  company, which is one of the Western
interests. A lot of the story revolves around  him and his relationship with Giorgio Viola,
who’s a hotel proprietor in the city,  and then also his wife and two daughters.
COWEN: I’ll add just a bit to that. This  novel comes out in 1904. It’s published
in serialized form. Today, it’s typically  considered to be Conrad’s greatest novel.
I think I agree with that assessment. It was  the British literary critic F. R. Leavis who
really resurrected the reputation of  this book, which for a long time was
ignored. It’s not short. In my edition, it’s  about 560 pages. I find it difficult to read,
but it’s one of my favorite novels. It would be  in, say, my favorite 50, maybe even my favorite
30. There’s a lot of different moving pieces. The  story does not always come in synchronous form.
It’s just, on purpose, a complicated story  because the world is a complicated world.
HANANIA: Yes. This is where you’re happy to have  AI because you could put things in there, and you
could say, “What does this mean? What is it about  this? What is this again?” Even the geography,
I thought, the first 30 pages or so, where it’s  telling you what Costaguana is, because all this
stuff is going to be very relevant for the plot.  I Googled Costaguana. What is a map? You got a
nice map online. Yes, you read it with some  aids to actually understand what’s going on.
COWEN: I’ll give you my answer afterward, but  tell me, you reading this for the first time
and then hearing it again on audiobook,  what most struck you about it? Maybe the
word surprise is a little too strong, but what  peaks your attention so much about Nostromo?
HANANIA: The political angle, I thought, was very  interesting in that I think of Latin American
dysfunction to be caused by socialism ideas  that started to take off in the 20th century,
in the second half of the 20th century. It is so  modern, even though the word socialism doesn’t
appear in the book until near the very end, or not  even the concept of socialism in any real sense.
Basically, you have these Western interests.  They’re doing things in the country. We’ll get
to this. I think it’s a very pro-business  book. Maybe I think a little bit of an
Ayn Rand with less caffeine or something like  that. It’s more realistic, more of a realist
novel. Yes, just how recognizable it is for anyone  who knows anything about Latin American history.
COWEN: The way I read Conrad, he’s clearly not  a socialist, but he views socialism as more of
a symptom than a cause. There’s this dead hand  of history and rent seeking and plutocracy and
corruption. Socialism is a particular later  form of that. Basically, the place is trapped,
and how effectively he portrays a trapped  society in a world where a lot of countries do
not develop very effectively. Though published  in 1904, again, to me also seemed remarkably
topical. If you were doing development  economics and you were to send people,
say, to five novels, A House for Mr. Biswas,  a few others, this would be one of the five.
HANANIA: Yes, I think that’s right. It’s  a timeless lesson in that these countries,
they need Western capital and Western  expertise in order to develop. The
problem is there’s nothing politically  less popular than just a bunch of rich
foreigners coming around and doing a bunch of  things. That’s easier to demagogue. That’s the
balance. It’s like the mind is bringing  development. It’s beloved in the region,
at least for the time. Whether that’s the case  in the long run, that’s one of the lessons of
the book. Then, at the same time, it’s just all  the discourse surrounding what’s going on there
is just hostile. They’re constantly fending off  threats to that ability to develop the country.
COWEN: Here’s one thing that struck me, and I’m  not sure you’ll agree. Early in the novel, there’s
all this talk about the Italians and Garibaldi and  liberty, and the extent to which I think this book
is also a critique of classical liberalism is what  surprised me reading it for the second time. The
first time was probably, I guess, 30 years ago,  that Conrad is not against the classical liberal
prescription, really, but he views it as another  pathology inserted into a hopeless situation.
It just morphs into some form of corruption and  interest groups. It’s replaced by the autocrats,
but it turns out to not really  matter more. There’s, again,
this dead hand of history. The indigenous  groups, their customs, their norms are
really what rule the area. The foreigners come  and go, and they may steal or extract wealth,
but at the end of the day, the talk of  liberty and democracy, for him, it’s a
kind of fraud. I think it’s also a recognition  that imperialism was not going to do the job.
HANANIA: Don’t you think that the Occidental  Province had a higher GDP per capita than the
rest of the country? It wasn’t just they made  money. It seems like there was real wealth.
Getting to the end, to the spoilers,  the miners actually march on the city
because they’re so loyal to Gould. They  like what’s going on. There is actual
improvement in people’s lives.  It’s not that nihilistic, right?
COWEN: It may be higher GDP, but keep  in mind GNP may be what counts. I don’t
think Conrad thought in those terms. I  don’t read him as a consequentialist,
though I’m mostly one myself. For  him, progress is about moral progress.
He doesn’t see a lot of moral progress in this  setting. The point that that’s not happening is,
for him, at least more important than,  oh, living standards went up a bit or,
well, isn’t this better than the even poorer  societies they had earlier on? I think he grew
up in what we now call Poland, but then was ruled  by Russia. The idea of foreign rule is something
he had such a strong instinctive dislike of. And  you see it in his other books as well that he’s
a cynic about foreign presence, though I don’t  think he’s saying things were better before.
HANANIA: No, I don’t think I agree.
COWEN: I didn’t think you would  agree. That’s why I said that.
HANANIA: There is a noble savage idea. There’s  one part where he goes into the rant when Sotillo,
the general, is torturing Hirsch. I  think he goes into a rant about how
primitive man did not devise as much sadistic  torture, which I don’t think is probably true,
but that’s Conrad’s idea. Basically,  there’s a kind of innocence there.
I look at the Hernandez and the robbers and the  people who are living in the countryside. Those
people are purest case of noble savage. There is  part of that. You’re right. Conrad is into honor.
This is a book about love and men caring about  women. There’s Monygham, the doctor’s loyalty
to Mrs. Gould, and then Decoud’s loyalty to  Antonia. His other books are about this. Yes,
he’s a romantic. He’s not a romantic in  politics. He thinks politics is a dirty—
COWEN: Agreed.
HANANIA: —unromantic world. If he thinks  socialism and populism on a scale of one
to 10 are like a one and classical liberalism  is a four, to me, he’s a classical liberal,
even though he’s not an eight or  a nine on classical liberalism.
COWEN: I think I read him as believing in  contingency as the most important truth
of politics and a geographic relativism. I  don’t think he has much Rousseau in him of
idealizing the noble savages, but he sees the  noble savages are not noble. They’re terrible,
but what’s terrible in them gets  recreated in us at higher levels
of wealth and power. That, for him, is  the most fundamental truth of politics.
HANANIA: There’s more of that  in the Heart of Darkness,
which is about a guy who just goes crazy  and becomes worse than the worst savage.
COWEN: It’s more explicit, I think.
HANANIA: Yes. Is it here, though? Is Gould a  savage? I think they come across well. I think
compared to the demagogues, compared  to the Montero, these half-literate,
various kind of guys who go around torturing  people and just trying to grab as much wealth
as possible—like Gould, what’s his biggest flaw?  He’s not emotionally expressive. There’s the sins
of the Western material interests just pale  in comparison to what the alternative is.
COWEN: I think Mrs. Gould comes across as fine.  Mr. Gould just seems captured by where he’s
lived for, what, now three generations. He’s a  pretend Englishman. I think it’s Conrad poking
fun at people who are actually Englishmen and  have not lived abroad for three generations,
but pointing out how quickly they  become corrupted by the places they go,
which for him would include Malaya,  India, many other locations.
HANANIA: What would a noncorrupt Gould  look like? What would he have done?
COWEN: Mrs. Gould is the noncorrupt Gould.  Again, I think she’s fine and nice enough—
HANANIA: Could she run the mine?
COWEN: —but has no power. No.
HANANIA: She couldn’t run the mine,
though. You won’t get a mine if  you won’t have someone like Gould.
COWEN: That’s right. That’s the contrast.
HANANIA: Can you run the mine and be better  than Gould in the way his wife is? No. It’s
a tragic situation, unquestionably. This  isn’t Ayn Rand. There’s so many hints of
it. I don’t know what Conrad’s influence  on Rand was, but this idea that we’re going
to destroy the world and break it down with  it, she must have gotten it from him, right?
I don’t know if it’s convergent evolution,  but it’s not as cartoonish. It is still
this man who can accomplish great things and  wants to be left alone. He doesn’t cheat his
workers. He doesn’t steal their money. He  doesn’t whip them. There’s none of this
other stuff that you find in people who  are more skeptical of Western interests.
COWEN: Keep in mind, the novel is named  Nostromo, not Gould. He’s the central
character. One thing that struck me is how  he has four different names. The first one,
Nostromo, it’s like nos, our man, you could  say, out of Italian and Latin. He’s presented
as our man. He turns out to be a fraud. He  doesn’t mind the notion of killing Hirsch or,
oh, if he’s tortured, maybe we don’t  really need to do that. He won’t bless
Mrs. Viola. He’s a bastard. He cares about  his own reputation. He becomes a thief.
His real name, Gianni Battista, gets  forgotten that he’s, in fact, from Italy,
is part of what’s forgotten in the novel,  just like Gould being originally English is
forgotten. For a while, he’s called Capataz  de Cargadores. He’s the man of capacity. He
gets things done. The novel’s always poking  fun at that version of Nostromo. Finally,
he’s called Captain Fidanza, captain of  faith. All the belief in him, all along,
was just that of faith. He’s a rotten guy  who’s a thief and doesn’t mind killing people.
HANANIA: Is he a rotten guy?
COWEN: He’s a rotten guy.
HANANIA: I don’t know. Is he a rotten guy? I  think Conrad admires him. He’s an antihero, right?
COWEN: Conrad always has a bit  of sympathy for the antihero.
HANANIA: You’re right. He’s a thief, but it’s the  most understandable, sympathetic kind of thievery
you can imagine. Everyone thinks this thing is  sunk. He’s basically sacrificed himself. He’s
vain. I think that’s his problem. He’s vain.  This is not seen, I think, as much of a sin in
Conrad’s time as it would be today. There’s  this idea that people basically care about
the reputation of others. It’s not like Battista  or Nostromo runs away from that. He admits that.
Then Viola, the wife, Teresa, thinks  he’s just a fool for this. Still,
it’s presented as an acceptable kind of  morality. There’s not a sadistic streak.
He’s poor. He’s poor up until the point  he gets tempted by the silver. He’s not
motivated by these venial concerns like these  generals are. He’s not self-sacrificial. He’s
not a saint or anything. I thought he was  a good guy. I don’t think he was a bad guy.
COWEN: No, I think he’s a bad guy.  Teresa has the best critique of him. Oh,
you just care what people think of you. People  are paid to praise you. You’re really a fraud,
she basically says. I think Conrad is showing  us he’s a victim of the place he moves to,
and he’s not any worse than what surrounds him.  He is, in essence, swallowed up by that world,
by the silver mine, by the culture surrounding  him. Just as Kurtz goes evil in Heart of Darkness,
Nostromo is in a less evil place, but he  goes corrupt. I think this is something,
maybe in a way, we’re supposed  to accept but not approve of.
HANANIA: I don’t know. What would virtue look like  to Conrad in someone in Nostromo’s situation? I
think that actually being brave, being the kind  of person that people look up to for a reason,
his reputation is an earned kind of reputation.  He’s known for being this guy who seduces women
and is brave and is taking care of  people. It’s the opposite of a toxic
masculinity. It’s a healthier masculinity  when you compare it to the other people
in the region. I think Nostromo is not an  intellectual, he’s not somebody like that, but
someone whose instincts and heart are basically  in the right place. I disagree strongly on this.
COWEN: His involvement with women, to me,
is a negative. He’s considering the two  Viola daughters. They’re called girls, right?
HANANIA: Yes.
COWEN: Now, your views on this may  not be the normal current views.
HANANIA: How old are they at the end,  by the way, when he’s about to marry?
COWEN: We don’t know. They’re called  girls and there is some passage of time,
but they’re not that old. I read Nostromo  again, this is guessing, as being in his
30s. He’s maybe a 37-year-old. He doesn’t  really relate to either girl as a human being.
HANANIA: This is the turn of the century.
COWEN: That Conrad is disapproving, and  it’s superficial, I think. There were
real love relationships in the story  elsewhere, even the Goulds, right?
HANANIA: Oh, yes.
COWEN: Or Decoud and the woman he’s in love  with. Nostromo has the worst relationship to
women. It’s all mediated through the father.  He treats the two as interchangeable. He’ll
pick at some point. He doesn’t love them. He  doesn’t care that they don’t love him. It’s at
best transactional or rooted in some desire for  sex or domination. Again, I think Conrad is not
simply a moralizing author, but he’s observing and  showing, and he’s not asking us to admire this.
HANANIA: No, I don’t think he’s asking us to  admire what’s going on with the girls. Yes,
you’re right. That’s a good point about  contrasting the relationships. I still
look at this as basically Nostromo’s  vain, stop the presses. We know that,
right? He’s not out there. There are worse  things you can be, right? You can imagine
someone being even worse with women. He  seems to want to leave them better off.
That one scene that there’s a striking  scene in the beginning where she’s like,
“Aren’t you my love, Nostromo, iron-red girl?”  My reading of that scene is that basically,
he wants to elevate her status. It’s a girl, maybe  he’s not in love with [her]. It’s not a big deal,
but he wants to make her feel good, and  he wants to give her the privilege of
having known Nostromo. He’s not sacrificing  his life to her and making her a wife and
having a traditional family and all that  stuff. Again, he’s vain. He’s a Playboy.
His heart is in the right place. I don’t  think there’s some terrible sin in that.
I think the Linda thing, where  he chooses the younger daughter,
I think it’s him being vain and wanting to  be unfettered. I feel like he was thinking
she was going to nag him for the rest  of his life. She loved him too much,
right? He wasn’t trying to hurt anyone, though.  He’s a limited character, but not a bad guy.
COWEN: Let me read you a quotation from  Charles Gould, which I think is important,
and you tell me what you think of it.  I quote, “He would blow everything up
from loyalty and from hate, from hate of  those liberals, as they call themselves,
liberals. The words one knows so well have a  nightmarish meaning in this country. Liberty,
democracy, patriotism, government, all of  them have a flavor of folly and murder.”
I think that’s Conrad telling us what  he thinks. Conrad wants to be a liberal,
broadly is a liberal, left Russian tyranny for  England, preferred England, but he goes around
the world, and he sees what those principles  are translating into, and he thinks that it
all does have the flavor of folly and murder.  What’s your take on that passage and my view?
HANANIA: I think you’re right. That is Conrad’s  view. Does that mean he thinks classical
liberalism is something that you shouldn’t  even bother trying to bring to the Third World,
or that’s something that is destined to end  terribly? I don’t know if it’s that cynical.
He has this phrase called Negro liberalism,  which I’d never heard before, which I’m not
sure exactly what it’s supposed to mean, but  to me that strikes me as it’s a bastardization.
